text:
Honestly... there seems to be a bad rep on the net for TKD. I know where it comes from, but TKD is much more than thatband so the bad rep is mistaken.  Many TKD kicks have produced KOs in MMA. I see no reason for any MMA fighter to not include a dozen or so good, effective TKD kicks into their bag of tools. The speed, intensity, athleticism, stance switching, etc., would also be good cross training. So why keep bagging on TKD?? Consider martial arts to be like college, with various traditional martial arts like a class that you can learn from.
Recently I saw a video of a guy that was incorporating Wing Chun hand techniques into his ground wrestling game. And it looked like it was working very well. But there is another martial art the keyboard warriors like to bag on for some reason.
Hell, playing soccer for 10 years would give you speed, endurance, kicking accuracy on a moving target, footwork, timing, and ability to stay on your feet when a tangle of legs is happening. Would be wonderful cross training, actually. But it's not even a martial art.
Less bagging and more training with an understanding of what you are gaining is what the pro's do. Jacket on, jacket off...

TKD shines with long reach and power kicks. I did boxing, TKD, and hapkido. In most of the street fights, people pull out their arms, try to punch or grab your opponent. That's the natural thing, and that's why we recommend boxing or judo for self defense. BUT, if you are able to kick at the situation, you will be the dominator. In TKD distance, the only working solution(if you're not possessing any weapon) is TKD. And most of the people(I can dare say all of the possible street fighters you can meet in your life) has no experience with blocking kicks. text:
To me, Taekwondo is a way to stay in shape, stay active, and still be an ordinary person. .. Im in school to be a nurse. Staying healthy will help me defend myself. I don't need the attention, and I'm not an aggressive person, nor am I competitive. But in class, I give it my personal best, and that is what matters to me. (I'll be 52 this month, and this one body has to last me the rest of my life.)
Also, my autistic son lives Taekwondo. I believe for him, he has the image that he's Chuck Norris when he's taking Taekwondo. He's 26 and doesn't get out for anything else. He is sociable with his classmates, and Taekwondo gives my son and I a bonding point.

text:
Hi, thanks for your video.  I started ITF TKD style in 1980, more for exercise, fitness and social activities.  I was taught traditionally by a Korean Master instructor.  The students had all the techniques explained and demonstrated by the instructor at each belt level.  Non-contact free sparring was introduced at green-belt.  The deliberate reason for non-contact sparring was/is rational.  "Do you really want to puposefully want to injure your sparring partner/friend?  It made sense to me then and still does as I'm not a sadistic person.  I love training to push myself to be more flexible and faster.  Everyone has their own physical and mental limits.  Of course, demonstrations are for promotion aspects and acrobatics achieve good audiences.  The performers skills are real but yes practised and choreographed.  TKD will prepare a person in life skills and self-defence.  As you go from white to black belt and beyond you learn new techniques at each stage.  So of the 100's of these, you may only use 3 in a real fight.  In my case it was 2 and 3 respectively.  In both real fights my first technique were a rising block against a) large stick and b) a Dropping fist.    2nd techniqe I used in both were a wrist twist to put my attackers off balance.  The first fight ended there as he was too surprised to continue.  The 2nd fight continued with my attacker trying to get me in a multitude of wrist locks.. my 3rd techniques were releases.  There was a 4th technique but nit TKD.. it was out of sheer boredom that I dug my finger nails into his forearm that led to him stopping his attack on me.  Those were what TKD has given me.  The ability to defend myself without a punch or kick.  After training hard for a long time, time will slow down in  when in a real fight and your decisions on which attack or defence tool to use will come very quickly.  All those technique repititions over the years become hard-wired into your brain and become automatic by your autonomous nervous system.  I believe the Japanese call it Mushin, "no mind".
Good luck with your journeys 🙏

text: 25+ years of taekwondo here, 4th dan (couldn't be bothered with racing the ranks), Australian champion (feather weight in 2004). Here is where I see taekwondo stands. You do tkd because you love they style, love the sport and love what it stands for. The comparison of what is the best, what is more effective in a street fight, is all rubbish and you shouldn't be doing martial arts if this is your mind set. After real life values, building up a successful company and earning myself time, the teachings of tkd (same as any other martial arts) teaches discipline and respect is the actual real life values that everyone should be chasing after. What's most important is that you enjoy your journey no matter what martial arts you do. Your values and enjoyment is important. Everything else is just external perspective and realistically, everyone else is already proud of your achievements, even if your don't realise, even as a beginner (you at least had the guts to make a start).

text:
In early 90s before TKD was an official Olympics sport, I was fin weight Canadian National Champion, and silver medal in Pan Am, and BC Provincial (twice) as well...I was lucky because competitor roaster was rather small back then.  I am grateful that I had an opportunity to compete, it is a good sport of discipline and other physical aspects, but I left TKD as I entered college and started focusing on other sport (I tore both hamstrings which never completely healed...it still hurts sometimes...).  We now compare it in this MMA dominated market for which is good in street fight...trust me, there is no such thing as good martial art for street fight (Krav Maga...maybe...but in street fight, anything goes).  Anyways, you are in a wrong place if you are learning TKD for street fighting...For self defense, it will help, but the best self defense is learning not to get into situation where you need self defense in first place.

Explantion for those who need it: taekwondo was not made for sport. It was made for soldiers. Hand techniques are lacking because soldiers have guns in their hands. Below I break down some basic taekwondo techniques and the real world purpose.

First, back fist and knife hands. Neither is a technique you want to be in a position to use; however, if an enemy grabs your barrel these techniques are game over. Letting go of your gun with your forward hand to prepare the strike, you pull your gun and your enemy toward you with your other hand as you strike. Freeing control of your barrel allowing you to perform taekwondo's ultimate move... the trigger pull.

Second, most taekwondo kicks while powerful are niche. Taekwondo is about establishing a standoff range with an enemy. As such the most effective and useful taekwondo combo is a straight front kick into a jumping front kick. If your enemy is in range to grab your weapon when you point it at them do this first. The first kick is to knock your enemy off balance hopefully preventing them from pointing their guns or knives at you, and the second is to deliver damage force. When done right your enemy will be knocked back to a safer distance allowing you to perform taekwondo's ultimate move... the trigger pull.

TLDR; Taekwondo wasn't made for sports or prolonged hand to hand combat. It is for Korean soldiers to use when necessary in warfare. It is far from useless in the real world.

Capoeira kicks can be used as surprise tactics in MMA, but in real life, if I get into a street fight, and I try to use the Capoeira approach by doing a Capoeira handstand kick, I might bruise my hand on the rough, rugged street concrete, and if the fight is in a rough alley, I might accidentally spin and knock into some dumpsters or any other environmental objects.

If my enemy is mad enough, he would shoulder ram me like a charging rugby player and I would fall down on my head, to be followed by a ground & pound style beating.

Of course, if you are on a smooth tile floor like in a subway station with lots of space, Capoeira might work.

As for my ITF Taekwondo approach, I could just back up to maintain distance and when he tries to close in on me, I can adapt by blocking his jab-cross, circle to his side and counter with a calf leg kick and jab to his face. Stepping back, I force him back with a push kick.

Tricking him with a jab feint, he dodges back with his hands up to protect his face, only for me to side kick his exposed stomach and knocking him down with a flying punch.

If someone mocks me and quote Mike Tyson by saying: "Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face", I'm just going to say at least my ITF TKD approach is easy enough for everyone to use and knock down a lone attacker in the streets, long enough to escape.

text:
1st kick: Great for a good ole feint and bait if you know your opponent likes to come in after the whiff (see how after the first turn, the opponent tries to capitalize but instead steps into the second oncoming shot?)

2nd kick: Double kick is great for catching your opponent off guard since most kicks are thrown one at a time and require a certain degree of "setup" to pull off. In that same vein, double kicking is fantastic for level changing kicks, as you'll notice the first kick is thrown low, which brings the opponent's attention low, and it does minimal damage, lulling the opponent into a false sense of security, and then the second kick is immediately whipped high at a much higher degree of force

3rd kick: The question mark kick is also a feint and bait type kick, where the initial chambering of the leg draws your opponent's attention low, making him believe you're about to attack his leg or body, and then immediately pivoting and extending to attack his head instead

4th kick: Despite her demonstrating the kick while standing in place (which shows great control on her part by the way), this kick is actually a fantastic way to close large distances while remaining dynamic and posing a threat. If you look at the example video afterward, the first stepping spin causes an opponent to back up, hesitate, or shield up (in this case, they backed up a bit and hesitated), and by the time you've spun around a second time for the kick, you've now closed a significant amount of distance to catch him with your shot (in this example, he realized his opponent's hands were low, so threw it at his head and caught him). Most people also tend to lower their hands when they believe they're out of range, so when you close the distance in such a rapid and unpredictable manner, you may be able to catch them before they can raise their guard in time, such as in this video here!

text: As a TKD Black Belt I think TKD is just another martial art that has become a victim of the sport and the “marketable consumer friendly martial art” package like Judo or Karate. The complete Martial Art like Karate for example is a useful art depending on intent. Dozens of kicks, all the punches found in Shotokan Karate and even Boxing, throws, etc. Context is everything. So many fighters from across the decades of full contact sports have made it work in their intended context. TL;DR I think the meme of “TKD doesn’t work” is just misinformed and the negatives of modern TKD are the same things that have brought down other traditional martial arts

text:
In the complete Kukkiwon curriculum(as defined in the Kukkiwon Textbook), the self-defense curriculum encourages high guard, boxing style punches and body movement, knees, elbows,  low kicks, takedowns and even limited groundwork and joint locks, and even modern training methods and more complete sparring. The problem is that 95% of what people are spending time on in Kukki Taekwondo clubs, is training for WT(F) style competition, since winning competition brings prestige to the school, and in the process they effectively ignore the rest of the system. 

If people had spent more time training the complete system, Kukki Taekwondo would NOT have had a reputation as such an incomplete martial art. text:
I love your respectful but truthful view. I've said things like this for years, and that is the art itself is fine, but the way it is generally taught is the problem... but it's only a problem if you take TKD for the purpose of fighting. Like you said, many people take TKD for fun or exercise, etc. They aren't looking to compete in something like MMA. And while a lot of people frown upon instructors being so lax in promoting their students, fact is, the instructor needs to make a living. Like it or not, the TKD instructor (unless he has income from elsewhere) is a businessman first, and a martial arts instructor second. He needs to be able to support himself and his family financially. That means attracting the most students as possible, and that means making the TKD school a place that attracts people of all ages, ability, etc. This is just the reality of it.

And yes, TKD guys can kick very hard. To say TKD is useless because Muay Thai students can kick harder misses a fundamental point. And that is there is only so much power one needs to knock someone out or break bones. This reminds me of in school how kids would say, 'I have a 9 mm" and the other kid says, "yeah, well I have a 45" but the point is both are deadly and it doesn't matter if one is more powerful than the other, you won't survive either one.

As for TKD sparring. TKD is trying to be a sport as much as a martial art. It's not as if the leaders of the leading TKD organizations don't realize that in real fights there is a lot of punching to the face or grabs/grappling/clinching. Of course they know that. But they are trying to make it a sport and aren't worried about practical fighting, anymore than boxers are worried that their sport isn't effective in a real fight. And the reason for what seems like ridiculous rules in Olympic TKD (no punching to the face, no leg kicks, etc) is because they're trying to make it unique sport, one that is and LOOKS different than kickboxing.

if someone wants to learn to actually fight, TKD in general isn't the place for you. And I can't blame them, if I were a TKD instructor, I wouldn't gear it towards fighters either, as that's not where the money is. And if I did happen to promote TKD for fighting purposes, the elephant in the room would be why someone wouldn't just join an MMA gym where they will learn a much more well rounded fighting system than TKD. So I say, join TKD but know you're doing it for similar reasons someone joins cardio kickboxing or joins boxing. To get in shape and have fun or because you like the unique sport of TKD. 

And another thing I do have to say, is that because TKD is so popular and attracts everyone from the soccer mom to the hardcore athlete, there is going to be a low level of proficiency in general because most people simply aren't very athletic or in good shape. So this means the average TKD fighter who gets in a fight (I'm not even talking about MMA) is usually someone who isn't very good at the art to begin with. I remember once I had a friend who told me he was almost a black belt and still got beat up in a fight. Well, I came to find out that by almost a black belt, he was only a green belt, and based on what his brother said, he didn't even fight back because he was one of those kids that was super timid and unathletic. But this is the type of story that happens all the time. I even remember once one kid in my TKD class was purposely slacking off and the instructor got fed up with him. And my instructor looked at him and said, "Do us all a favor, if you get in a fight and get beat up, don't say TKD doesn't work."

TKD ruleset encourages you to be precise, fast, and to properly connect your attacks, with less emphasis in hitting the head and grappling out of the equation. text:
Hi Rob, thank you for this analysis. I practice taekwondo (tkd) and I would like to add some comments to what you said. There are 3 types of tkd: WT taekwondo, the Olympic style, ITF taekwondo the traditional style and the style I practice, and the ATA, the American version of taekwondo, which alas, I know very little about. I would like to clarify that WT competitions are full contact fights, like most of the fighting sports and, although ITF competitions are semi-contact fights, I saw many concussed people during all the events I took part to (and some K.O. too...not mentioning countless bruised and broken ribs). When it comes to power, during ITF competitions there is a session called power breaking during which the participants have to break special plastic boards that are about 1 inch thick and for adults black belts the boards are two. You need to break these boards using hands and/or kicks. These boards are designed to break only if you strike with the right amount of power (a lot of it!) and on precise spots. There are many videos on YouTube if you want to have a look at it (just type in ITF breaking competitions). Lastly, hands, in ITF tkd we use punches a lot. This style, in fact, is very similar to kick boxing (not very similar though) alternating hands and kicks.
So as you can see tkd (especially the ITF) it's not too watered down since it is highly regulated (at least here in Europe) and if you do not meet the standards for a black belt you simply fail your grading (usually panels have external examiners).
Kicks are not too weak considering the power breaking competitions and the amount of injures I witnessed during competitive sparring.
Hands are used a lot in ITF, not as much as muay-thai, but still a lot!

text: First, I am sad to say that you are right across the board. I have been practicing TKD since 1972 (now that is back in the day). Tournaments were all open tournaments AND there was no safety equipment. There was crazy rules like no contact to the face or head, unless the opponent was rushing in. So you can imagine what happened. People were getting their clock cleaned as they rushed in. I did it myself and got booed by the crowd in Gainesville because I nailed the guy as he rushed in. In general, you got a point by demonstrating that you could have followed through with the kick or punch. If your arm was fully extended then no point. I believe that despite the constraints of the early tournaments, we had more control of our kicks and punches. Paradoxically, in a street fight switching to full contact was not that hard. Because either way you had to hold it or let it go. I proved it in a few street fights. Naturally, some people got taken off the mat on stretchers so there was a cost to the lack of safety equipment. So I was around when sport TKD became the be all end all. Examinations went from one on one to group examinations were almost everyone passed. We passed kids all the way to black belt and they couldn't fight for real. And as soon as they got in a real fight and lost they quit TKD. My nephew was one of those. text:
Good summary. Joe Rogan talks about this and his breakdown is similar. I am 50 and train TKD with my 9 year old daughter. There is value in isolating on only high kicking to learn that one skill really good. We both do the Olympic style sport sparring. It is hard to learn to kick someone successfully who is fully trying to stop you and only has to worry about above the waist kicks.

Yes, the hands are low and that isn’t really actively taught it is just the best way to do it when you are only sparring with kicks. Sparring like this also forces you to solve problems with kicks. Many people do charge forward to close range where kicking high is very tough. You need to move/kick your way out of it (though it is possible to pick up 1 point for a single punch to the chest..this is lower points than any kick). You are also encouraged to try tougher kicks as they score more. 

Last thought, our daily training is all kicking drills with someone holding either a kicking pad or target and always moving in some way, usually forward or backward just due to practicality. We do learn to kick full force just don’t spar that way.

text:
I’ve been doing TKD for 5 years and these are my two biggest takeaways:

1) It depends on where you train. Some places are serious about teaching you how to fight and some places are what we call “McDojos”. 

2) It depends on the martial artist. I’ve met ‘black belts’ who can barely kick above their waist. I’ve met guys who I could probably beat up even without 5 years of experience. But I’ve also met guys who would knock me out cold in no more than five seconds. If you’re serious about learning how to fight well, that will transfer into your training. For example, I train in sparring, endurance, agility and strength whereas other students just show up, do the kicks and leave. 

At the end of the day, if you’re serious about becoming a good fighter and if you have a good coach, TKD is an excellent martial art. But there are a lot of those who train and are honestly incompetent.

I applaud this analysis.  I received a black belt in TKD in 1980, before it became a sport. I was trained by a former Golden Gloves boxer and wrestling coach, who himself was trained in TKD, as a social worker in narcotics rehabilitation, by New York City narcotics detectives. His partner was a former Green Beret who served two tours in Vietnam. To assume that these men couldn't fight because they were TKD practitioners would be idiotic. If you train for tournaments, as you say, that's fine, but that is what you are doing. The strength and variety of TKD kicks make it an extremely valuable skill set if you train to fight for real. It helps to cross train, but that's true for all martial arts. That's because in the end, a martial art style is simply a platform to learn technique, and that's it. Good instructors teach tactics, and tactics win fights. 

And as you say, train to fight in TKD and train to hit with balance, speed, precision and timing, and you will hit like a truck. I've been on both ends of those kicks, so I definitely know what I'm talking about there.

text:
I'm an ITF Taekwon-do black belt (3rd dan) from Europe. TKD was originally intended to destroy or break your opponent with a single well placed attack with the right "weapon" on a weak point to your opponent's body. Like a knife hand thrust to the throat or an elbow to the solar plexus.

Ice cold showers and conditioning/hardening of your fists, forearms, legs and shins is mandatory if you practice by the book. Original TKD comes from Kyokushin Karate and was thought to the Korean military as a last resort. It was feared by the Vietcong.

This all changed when it became a sport. Low kicks were banned from competitions and it became semi contact due to the many injuries in competition. Schools focus mainly on competition sparring and tactics to score points - like skipping around on one leg with the other raised to make quick side kicks. The tappy tap stuff.

Many techniques are still there in the Tuls (patterns), but less and less people know the applications for self defense. Original TKD has throws, joint locks, submissions, rolls, ground fighting, elbows, knees, low kicks and even defending yourself while sitting on a chair.

WTF TKD is a whole other story though.

text:
Thank you for pointing out the main purpose of competition Taekwondo: is a competition of your feet (boxing with your feet). Competition Taekwondo was never meant to be the ultimate form of self-defense. 

While traditional Taekwondo is useful for a wide range of fighting skills, competition Taekwondo is more of a contest, maybe the most enjoyable and technical contest that exists today. Purposely removing the function of punches allows a person to throw a lot more kicks and much more complicated kicks. And just like kicking is not allowed in boxing, punching is very limited in Taekwondo.

Furthermore, a person well trained in Taekwondo who learns western boxing and some grappling will have a huge advantage in a real fight over someone who never learned taekwondo . Also practicing the Forms and hand strikes in taekwondo and practicing them in application is an excellent form of self defense when incorporated witht the kicks. 

Taekwondo as a self-defense is making a comeback, the focus is not only on WT competition anymore. In the coming years you are going to see many more hand strikes and self-defense techniques in Taekwondo

As a ITF TKD practitioner, I agree there are a lot of MDojos out there. As to kicks are weak? I beg to differ. We break boards starting at White belt. By the time you test for upper color belts, you’re doing “flying” sidekicks through 4-5 boards handheld. For 1st Dan, I had a standing sidekick through 5 boards, no spacers. Yes the kicks can be wicked tough,  it as you said, you have to train for it. Power breaking is one of the toughest events in our tournaments. You punch, sidekick, roundhouse (turning kick), and reverse turning kick through stacks of 5-7 boards depending on rank. As to your last point… in ITF we use our hands, and a lot. In sparring we punch to the head & face. Yes we have kicks, but we have hands too. WT Taekwando (Olympics) typically does not use hands and are more leg centric.  And before anyone says I don’t know better because I do Taekwando… I also studied both Shotokan Karate & Gosoku-ryu under Master Charles Scott who studied under Master Kubota. 

There are advantages and disadvantages to each style, and they all have something to bring to the table.

text:
Good video. Just adding some extra info as a TKD practitioner (10 years of practice).

One small thing to add, generally I feel like your legs tend to be stronger than your arms. You walk on your feet all day, but not your hands. I think TKD was smart about the decision to favor a stronger long ranged weapon. For someone who has less upper body strength, using kicks can be helpful. Also, we do practice punches and a small variety of hand techniques in TKD.

In self defense, your goal is to get as far away from the opponent as possible, so you have more time to run. You also never know if the person attacking you has a weapon, so it is safer to keep a distance. Also, at a longer distance you have more time to react to your opponents movements.

For those saying TKD may struggle at a closer range, TKD does have some close range kicks to the head, like crescent kicks :)

text:
I wholeheartedly agree that many traditional martial arts paths have become diluted over time. The numbers themselves are telling. World Taekwondo (WT), one of the sport's largest governing bodies, reports approximately 80 million practitioners globally, while another source, the World Taekwondo Organization (WTO), claims that number exceeds 200 million. We must question if there are truly that many qualified teachers to support such a massive number of students. If not, this presents the first major issue.

Investing in a black belt can be a significant financial commitment, often costing ten thousand dollars or more. Much like buying a new car or a house, this isn't a decision you should make based on convenience, such as the studio's schedule or proximity to your home. You are paying for a teacher, and that instructor should be focused on teaching, not on profiting excessively from hidden fees and high student turnover, which can often be signs of a flawed ideology.

This leads to a crucial distinction: self-defense and fighting are not the same.

Gichin Funakoshi, the founder of modern Shotokan karate, believed the ultimate goal of karate was to improve a practitioner's character, not simply to prepare for physical combat. His philosophy centered on the idea that training should instill virtues like respect, discipline, and humility to create better individuals.

In contrast, Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) training is designed to prepare a fighter for a real, unpredictable combat scenario. This involves full-contact sparring, where techniques are tested against a resisting opponent. Many traditional martial arts, however, often emphasize forms (katas) and pre-arranged drills with limited or no full-contact sparring. This difference in training can leave practitioners unprepared for the chaos and pressure of an actual fight.

MMA also values versatility. A fighter specializing in a single discipline, like boxing, may be an expert at punching but is vulnerable to takedowns and grappling. Conversely, a fighter who only practices a grappling art like Judo might excel at throws but be at a disadvantage against a skilled striker. MMA forces fighters to be proficient in all ranges of combat—standing, in the clinch, and on the ground—making them more adaptable to any situation.

The goal of karate is self-defense, not necessarily to fight a trained opponent. We can explore extremes to illustrate this point: could a 90-pound girl with a decade of MMA experience stop a prime Mike Tyson from taking her purse? At some point, the answer is no. MMA, which has evolved during my lifetime (I was born in 1967), is simply mixed martial arts, and I understand the arguments well.

Not everyone is a twenty or thirty-year-old in peak physical condition who can survive a full-on MMA fight; even many of those who compete don't do well. I started with Tae Kwon Do before moving to Tang Soo Do, but the two-hour commute from my country home made it unsustainable. I later joined an MMA gym opened by a local Alabama fighter not far from my job. I fought four times and quickly discovered it wasn't for me.

After that, I worked with a private trainer, moved back here, and then hired another private trainer before finally committing to a studio to earn my black belt. I wanted to achieve it before I was too old and finally settled in one place long enough to complete the journey. I've also studied boxing and kickboxing, as well as Japanese sword, though not in the most traditional sense.

I took Kenpo from a former world champion and hall-of-fame member and found that the program for earning a black belt was different from the program for sparring and competing. In my opinion, the belt curriculum, which was devised by the Traceys based on Ed Parker’s work with some tweaks, differed greatly from the fighting and sparring curriculum designed by Joe Lewis, a legendary martial artist and kickboxer.

Lewis developed a fighting system based on 25 principles he believed were crucial for success in combat. These principles are rooted in efficiency, strategy, and a blend of mental and physical preparation.

Setups: Confusing an opponent physically and mentally by practicing timing, distance, and using misleading body language.

Positioning: Maintaining a relaxed state for explosive power while staying assertive to control the fight.

Independent Movement: A strike should move independently of the body to eliminate "leading centers" and make movements more deceptive.

Initial Speed: The ability to relax and explode into action, which is more important than overall speed.

Critical Distance Line: Understanding the opponent's effective range to position yourself defensively and offensively.

Line of Attack: The three primary routes to a target: inside, outside, and middle.

Bridging the Gap: Effectively closing the distance using initial speed and proper footwork.

Five Primary Techniques: Lewis’s core techniques: the sidefist/backfist, inverted close punch, reverse punch, side kick/roundhouse kick, and spinning rear kick.

Leading Side vs. Rear Side: Using techniques from the leading side for greater economy of motion and speed.

Economy of Motion: Prioritizing the most direct, straight-line route to the target.

Relaxation vs. Tension: Relaxation is key to speed and energy conservation, while tension slows you down and makes you predictable.

Mobility vs. Immobility: Using various footwork techniques to create unpredictability.

Extension, Hyperextension, Double Hyperextension: Increasing your reach to extend your own critical distance line.

Leading Centers: Eliminating tell-tale movements that give away your next move, or using them intentionally for faking.

Unpredictability vs. Classical Form: The importance of not being predictable by varying rhythm, angle, and using feints.

Straight Line vs. Curved Line: The straight line is the most direct and powerful route to a target.

Body Rhythm vs. Broken Rhythm: Using fluid, continuous motion versus interrupted, unpredictable motion to disorient an opponent.

The Three-Point Principle: Keeping three points of the body stable for readiness to attack or defend.

Forward Pressure: Continuously moving forward to overwhelm an opponent psychologically and physically.

Half-Commitment vs. Full-Commitment vs. Extension-Commitment: Committing to a strike with different degrees of force and follow-through.

Attack by Combination: Using a combination of strikes to overwhelm defenses.

Attack by Interception: Attacking an opponent as they are attacking you to neutralize their offense.

Feinting: Using deceptive movements to create an opening.

Deception and Faking: Using a range of misleading actions to trick an opponent into making a mistake.

The Law of the Lead Hand and Foot: The leading hand and foot should be the primary tools for probing, controlling distance, and initiating attacks.Today at 58 I am a Shotokan student and hope to get a black belt here as well before I get to old

One cralification i would like to add though is how points are scored in sparring, and how it has changed in the past 15ish years. In modern tkd sparring (olympics) the hogu (chest protector) has pressure censors in it to auto add point when the amount of force passes a certain threshold, so weak kicks will not score. This however had the unfortunate side effect of changing what moves are effective, and making it look (and feel tbh) like tag with your feet.  
Prior to about 2010-2012ish tkd sparring was a lot more "physical" and had a lot more knockouts.  A large majority of non-olympic level tkd athletes agree, this older style was much better, and more "realistic".  The amount of knockouts, tkos, and even a few broken ribs I witnessed in this era can easily attest that tkd kicks are far from weak.

text: there's two different styles in TKD that is WTF vs ITF. WTF style is the most popular around the world. They focus more on balance and technique to score points hence its what is used in the Olympics so this style isnt recommended for combat. However,  ITF style typically called "North Korean TKD" (idk why they call it that, ITF was developed in the south) focuses more to combat styles. In sparring they dont use pads or any protective gear and their goal is to KO their opponent cleanly. ITF TKD is what south Korean special forces practice mainly therefore TKD is Deeply rooted in the military. Even in MMA TKD has a special move that allows the user to have their backs completely turned to their opponent and that is the famous "spinning back kick"

text: Learning to Kick is one of the skills I am most thankful for when I trained in TKD - the skills carried over into Muay Thai and other percussive arts. When training in TKD you must be honest and aware of the issues concerning TKD’s shortcomings in other fighting ranges (grappling, trapping and punching ranges and of course weapons range). You will learn the proper delivery of power from the feet, hips and legs. To keep you honest it is a good idea to add another art with an emphasis in a different range - boxing and wrestling are great add ons to help you in other ranges. If you are training Kyokoshin Kai Karate I feel boxing and wrestling is still a great adjunct to help your other ranges. Still, Boxing and TKD are a great together as the footwork are very complementary.

I did karate for a year or so. Never really got into it. Im in muay thai now and I definitely see a lot of flaws with karate. The blocking first of all is terrible, if you block a jab with a traditional block in karate, it leaves you open for a hook that a quick muay thai fighter will have no challenge landing. Secondly the kicking in karate is actually pretty lame. The reason is because when they kick, they immediately snap there legs back. Basically the kick lands with the shin bone but immediately gets pulled away. And not only that, but there isnt much power in karate kicks because they dont really use their hips. They just kinda throw there leg out there, and immediately snap it back as soon as their kick touches their opponent.

In muay thai, you use your hips to land a completely disabling kick to the body or the head or leg. When you kick in muay thai, you dont immediately snap back your leg. You drive your leg through your opponent basically imagining that you are trying to cut them in half. Not only that but the power comes from the hips, you arent just extending your leg and immediately bringing it back like karate.

I also think the conditioning in general in muay thai is way more significant than what i experienced in karate.

So yeah, my conclusion is that a muay thai fighter would absolutely cripple a karate fighter, or a taekwondo fighter.

Tae also has knees and elbows in their syllabus. But I understand why you gave the point to MT cos  they are not used as often as MT. With experience of both, my bias will put my personal W to tae. Mainly because I feel it's easier for tae to transition to MT but not vice versa. (Not saying it's not possible)

At the same time, I absolutely HATE how people start to shit on Tae based on what they watch in the Olympics. Like yeah, WT sparring is in a sorry state, and MT is violent and brutal, but being brutal does not mean it's better. Tae has potential to be brutal af too. The kicks can be just as powerful. But unlike MT, where the power comes from raw strength of the fighter, tae harnesses the power from the speed and momentum of the pivoting of our hips, the snapping notion of their kicks and as well as the spin. Plus, it was widely effective in Vietnam, where US soldiers reported that they had to pick up bodies with "necks broken and caved in ribs" after their korean counterparts fought the viet cong in CQB.

Japan tried to erase Korean culture and forbid Taekkyon masters from teaching it and if they wanted to continue, they had to teach Karate.  So Karate format such as dojo and belt system was adapted but they still emphasized kicks.  Which is why Taekwondo kicks are similar to Taekkyeon kicks.  Karate used to be mostly hands and front kicks only.  They didn't have spinning kicks or roundhouse kicks back then.

text:
as basic information, Tae Kwondo is divided into 2 streams, namely the first ITF and the second WTF - Kukkiwon.. ITF is the origin of the original flow of Tae Kwondo.. But Te Kwondo is actually Korean Karate which is called Tang Soo Do and combined with martial arts that developed in Korea both from Japanese and traditional influences as well as Chinese martial arts, such as Taekkyeon, Soo Bhak Do, Hapkido, Hwa Rang Do, Kuk Sul Won and so on which were then united and nationalized in 1950 by General Choi Hon Hi under the ITF. which later developed into KTA and WTF in the 1970s.. you need to know Tae Kwondo itself is a development of Tang Soo Do -Korean Karate in which practitioners, instructors and students are Korean citizens who study in Japan. and Tang Soo Do - Tae Kwondo is actually a Shotokan Karate style. So it's no wonder there are many similarities in Movement in Tul, Poomsae, Tae Geuk, Hyeong, Dongjak/Basic between Tae Kwondo and Tang Soo Do with Karate especially Shotokan.. 
these are the 9 Kwans which pioneer of Tae Kwondo.

Song Moo Kwan(송무관) - first of the original kwans, founded in Kaesong on March 20,1944 by Ro Byung Jik(노병직), who had studied karate under Gichin Funakoshi along with Chung Do Kwan founder Lee Won Kuk in Japan.

Chung Do Kwan(청도관) - second kwan dojang in Korea founded in September, 1944 by Lee Won Kuk(이원국). He studied Taekkyeon in Seoul, He also studied Shotokan Karate in Japan, Kung Fu in Henan and Shanghai in China, and other.[

Moo Duk Kwan(무덕관) - was founded in 1945 by Hwang Kee(황기) teaching Hwa Soo Do. Hwang studied Taekkyon, T'ai chi and some types of Kung Fu in China. His first two attempts at running a school of Hwa Soo Do were unsuccessful. After 1946, realizing that most Koreans were unfamiliar with the Chinese-based arts he was teaching, he incorporated the more familiar, Japanese influenced, Tang Soo Do into his curriculum. By 1953 and onward until 1960, the Moo Duk Kwan had risen to become biggest martial arts organization in Korea, with close to 75% of all martial artists in Korea practicing Tang Soo Do Moo Duk Kwan. In 1957, Hwang made a discovery of Soo Bahk(수박), a traditional Korean martial art from Muyedobotongji(무예도보통지). In 1960, the Korean Soo Bahk Do (수박도) Association was incorporated and officially registered with the Korean government as the traditional Korean martial art. The following year, the Moo Duk Kwan Soo Bahk Do discipline was recognized internationally for the first time.

Ji Do Kwan(지도관) - Chosun Yun Mu Kwan Kong Soo Do Club (조선연무관 공수도부, Chosun Yun Mu Kwan had been the original Japanese Kodokan Judo school in Korea for over 30 years previously) founded March 3, 1946 by Chun Sang Sup(전상섭), who had studied Shotokan karate with Gichin Funakoshi in Japan, and later called his art 'Kong Soo Do(공수도)'. He had a very close relationship with Yoon Byung-In, founder of YMCA Kwon Bop Club. Chun and Yoon would travel to train with other martial artists, sometimes traveling to Manchuria. They trained with each other so much that they became known as brothers. Chun went missing during the Korean War; subsequently, this kwan voted to change its name to 'Jidokwan'. After Chun disappeared in Korean War, the original students of Chun voted Master Yoon Kwe-byung(윤쾌병, Trained Chuan Fa in Manchuria) as Jidokwan 1st President.

Chang Moo Kwan(창무관) - YMCA Kwon Bop Club(YMCA 권법부) founded in 1946 by Yoon Byung-in(윤병인), who had studied Chinese Kung Fu (Quan fa). When he studied in Nihon University, he trained Shudokan karate under grandmaster Kanken Tōyama.[ Unlike other taekwondo kwans, early Chang Moo Kwan was mainly based on Chinese Kung Fu (Quan-fa). The early Chang Moo Kwan taught Palgi kwon(팔기권) (which influenced by Bajiquan).[ Yoon went missing during the Korean War. His teachings were carried on by his top student Lee Nam Suk, who changed the name of the school to Chang Moo Kwan. 10th Dan Grandmaster Soon Bae Kim is one of two Kukkiwon 10th Dans in charge of Kukkiwon testing.

Han Moo Kwan(한무관) - founded in August 1954 by Lee Kyo Yoon as an offshoot of the Yun Moo Kwan/Jidokwan. 

Oh Do Kwan(오도관) - founded in 1955 by Choi Hong Hi, who also became honorary head of the Chung Do Kwan. Top instructors were Nam Tae Hi and Han Cha Kyo.

Kang Duk Won(강덕원) - founded in 1956 by Park Chul Hee and Hong Jong Pyo as an offshoot of the Kwon Bop Bu/Chang Moo Kwan.

Jung Do Kwan(정도관) - founded in 1956 by Lee Yong Woo (died August, 2006) as an offshoot of the Chung Do Kwan.

The Kwans united in 1955 as Tae Soo Do. In the beginning of 1957, the name Taekwondo was adopted by several Korean martial arts masters, for its similarity to the name Tae Kyon.

General Choi established ITF-Taekwondo (which practices a   more traditional form of taekwondo) while WTF-Taekwondo   (which has a strong emphasis on sparring) became an Olympic sport in 2000.

A goodwill trip to North-Korea in 1966 caused General Choi to fall in disgrace in the eyes of the South-Koreans. Choi resigned as president of the K.T.A. and founded the I.T.F. on March, the   22nd of that same year. The headquarters of ITF was established in Canada.

ITF started concentrating on the forms developed by General   Choi, while the KTA (which later, on May 28, 1973, became the WTF) concentrated on the Palgwe’s. Later the WTF abandoned the Palgwe’s and started concentrating on Taeguks. Slowly, the WTF emphasis turned to sparring. This is also the reason why a lot of people call (WTF) Taekwondo a ‘Martial Sport’ rather than a ‘Martial Art’.

text:
I started as a kid with shotokan karate but I had a terrible teacher which made me drop martial arts for around 22 years. Then I picked up boxing and fell in love with it, while adding taekwondo to work on my legs some more. Taekwondo is a bit too similar to karate for my taste, but the difference is clear- keeping distance, looking for openings and delivering precise strikes. You chamber kicks to make the opponent guess which kick you perform, to fake kicks or to just kick again. It requires a ton of balance and speed compared to karate. It's pretty negligent on hands but it's not an issue for a boxer, since boxing strikes make karate ones look like jokes anyway.

Karate is more balanced than taekwondo when it comes to using hands and feet, there is a lot of focus on front-back movement while being well balanced in order to get more power. When it comes to styles of boxing- taekwondo is like outboxing while karate is like inboxing, both require a lot of movement but in a very different way.

All that being said- when it comes to the "art" of "martial arts" both aint got shit on northern kung fu styles. These are some of the most beautiful movements a human body can perform

Karate is a Japanese martial art focusing heavily on powerful hand strikes, blocks, and low stances. In contrast, Taekwondo is a Korean martial art that prioritizes fast, acrobatic, and high-flying kicks. While Karate offers a balanced split of hands and feet, Taekwondo relies about 70% on kicking.Key DifferencesOrigin: Karate originated in Okinawa, Japan, rooted in traditional Zen philosophy. Taekwondo was developed in Korea, emphasizing dynamic movement and modern athleticism.Technique: Karate focuses on a balanced mix of punches, elbows, and kicks, with rigid stances to deliver maximum power. Taekwondo heavily emphasizes agility, flexibility, and dynamic footwork.Competitions: Karate tournaments often involve kata (forms) and kumite (point/continuous sparring). Taekwondo is an Olympic sport governed by World Taekwondo (WT) or the International Taekwondo Federation (ITF), emphasizing dynamic, fast-paced sparring.Self-Defense: Karate provides a more versatile approach to close-range combat. Taekwondo teaches students to maintain distance using rapid kicking.Which Should You Choose?Choose Karate if: You want a well-rounded, full-body workout that balances punches and kicks, and you appreciate traditional, foundational discipline.Choose Taekwondo if: You love flashy, high-impact kicks, want to develop explosive leg strength, or are interested in Olympic-style competitive sparring.

Everybody shit-talks these kind of competitions because they´re "not real". Of course they´re not. These are trained men, they can hurt each other really badly if they where to fight as a mad-man.
I´m a boxer, have been for 4 years. I know my share of dealing and receiving damage to both body and head. I´ve fight on the streets 6 times, "won" all of them, and although my training was the main reason I didn´t get beaten in those 6 fights, none of them resembled anything to my numerous fights on the ring. On the street I don´t have my gloves, so every punch I land will hurt me, a head´s a fucking hard thing if you hit it hard bare-handed. My speed and combos have to be different for this reason. I´m also exposed to headbuts, elbows, bites, kicks to the groin, grappling, etc. When I train, I do it to go the distance, for me that means 24 to 30 minutes of fighting. On the streets, a long fight doesn´t lasts longer than 3 minutes, and at least one of them will be starring and trash-talking. And I´ve managed to stay on foot and "win" those bouts.
People often think that just because the real fighting conditions are different from those on a dojo or a gym, the trained fighter will lose because he´s not used to that. Bullshit. You think your un-trained ass can beat a professional fighter just because suddenly you are allowed to bite his dick off or try to poke out his eyes? You won´t, and will probably get your shit broken in several pieces. There´s absolutely no challenge for me in going to a bar and pick a fight with a sad slob who has probably never learn how to defend himself. I like to fight with people on extremely similar conditions than me, so I can test my skills properly
Now, about the styles. Some are better against others, but mainly is because of the fighter. Thinking than on a given situation a Karate master would get beaten sense-less by a Muay-Thai guy is useless, because that is highly unlikely to happen. That shit only happens in movies. In the street, most of the fights will be between two slobs, or one unlucky fuck and a trained person. I know I can beat to a pulp several TDK or Karate practitioners. not because their style is inferior than mine, but because I´m extremely conditioned, I take my training seriously and besides training to master my martial art of choice, I do it so my body is able to react the way I want it to and I know for a fact that many traditional martial artists take this part for granted, and only focus on mastering their style. Still, I also know there are several traditional martial artists that can turn my face into a Picasso, and that doesn´t means boxing sucks, or that it doesn´t works on real fights.
The moral of this (from a simple boxer like me), pick a style you like, train, fight with real fighters, not your high-school fat bully, but people who are currently training. Maybe that way people will focus on their own body and craft, instead of being keyboard warriors.

The biggest problem in Taekwondo is the excessive jumping and kicking, which is quite a burden on physical strength. If you can't take advantage of the speed and kicking to knock out your opponent in the early stages of the game, you will face a decrease in physical strength.
Otherwise, you will have a more comprehensive and rigorous physical training to ensure that you always have enough strength to jump and kick, once the physical strength is exhausted, your speed no longer has an advantage, and the strength is not enough to knock out the opponent.
But it's almost impossible to do that. At high intensity, if your opponent is at a similar level to you, you'll lose a lot of energy in less than five minutes, yet your opponent will probably still have more than half the energy to handle you.

text: Their description isn't at all like the TKD I learned and got my black belt in. We do use a lot of kicks because they have longer reach and our legs tend to be stronger than our arms. But we also do a ton of punches as well as throws. I could never imagine fighting as the guys do at 1:39 where they are chest-to-chest but still kicking. This video seems to be focusing on the "point sport" of TKD rather than as a martial art or form of self-defense. This is the problem with turning anything into a sport. The kicks look cool, so tournaments make them the only way to score points. But there's no point system in real sparring, at least not in the school I was in 25 years ago.  We put on pads and we fought.  If someone was getting pummeled or got hit really hard, our sensei would call "break" and give that person some advice and a moment to recover. In general sparring, we didn't declare a "winner." Even in most belt tests, you were judged on how you fought, and not on points.

text:
While it is a historical fact that Taekwondo was influenced by Karate, it cannot be dismissed as a mere "derivative" or "copycat" martial art. This is because Taekwondo has evolved in a completely different direction in terms of technical principles, body mechanics, and core philosophy.
​Although Taekwondo may have adopted a formal motif from Karate, it has completely overhauled the "engine" (the principles of power generation), the exterior (kicking techniques), and the "driving style" (competition rules) to align with the dynamic spirit of the Korean people.
​The fact that modern Karate is now adopting Taekwondo’s signature techniques is the most definitive evidence that Taekwondo has moved far beyond Karate’s sphere of influence, establishing its own unique "martial superiority."

The Evolution of Taekwondo: From Influence to Innovation and Karate’s Adoption
​Creation of Multi-dimensional and Spinning Kicks:
While Karate kicks were traditionally single-strike attacks from a grounded stance, Taekwondo opened a new dimension by combining weight shifting with aerial maneuvers. Techniques like the Narae-chagi (Double Kick)—delivering multiple strikes in mid-air—and the 360-degree Spinning Kicks are original assets of Taekwondo. Today, elite WKF (World Karate Federation) athletes actively adopt and practice these Taekwondo-style mechanics to score high points in competition.

​Establishment of the Unique 'Bounce Step':
Taekwondo perfected the 'Bounce Step,' a rhythmic, light-footed movement used to control distance and timing, similar to fencing. This is a complete departure from the static stances of traditional Karate. Modern Karate sparring (Kumite) now frequently features practitioners using these light, Taekwondo-style steps to find angles, proving that Karate has integrated Taekwondo's superior footwork for modern sport.
​Shift in Striking Paradigm via Body Protectors (Hogu):
The introduction of body protectors in the early 1960s evolved Taekwondo from a 'stop-impact' art into a 'full-impact' combat sport. This environment allowed for the development of bolder, more explosive techniques. The sheer power and speed of these full-contact kicks established a unique identity for Taekwondo that has now become a benchmark for kicking excellence worldwide.

text:
Etymology - 

Kalaripayattu is a martial art which developed out of combat-techniques of the 11th-12th century battlefield, with weapons and combative techniques that are unique to Kerala. The word Kalaripayattu is a combination of two Malayalam words - kalari (training ground or battleground) and payattu (training of martial arts), which is roughly translated as "practice in the arts of the battlefield".

History -

According to legend, Parashurama, the sixth avatar of Vishnu, learned the art from Shiva, and taught it to the original settlers of Kerala shortly after bringing Kerala up from the ocean floor.[note 1] A song in Malayalam refers to Parashurama's creation of Kerala, and credits him with the establishment of the first 108 kalaris throughout Kerala, along with the instruction of the first 21 Kalaripayattu gurus in Kerala on the destruction of enemies.[5]

According to another legend, Ayyappa, a war deity from Kerala, learned Kalaripayattu in the Cheerappanchira Kalari in Muhamma.

Karate focuses on powerful, linear hand strikes and stable stances, while taekwondo emphasizes fast, dynamic, and high-flying kicks.Karate TechniquesPunches and Strikes: Uses linear, direct punches (like the straight punch or oizuki) driven by hip rotation and body weight.Hand Defenses: Relies heavily on strong, hard blocks (maki) and open-hand strikes like the knife-hand (shuto).Stances: Utilizes low, grounded, and wide stances for maximum stability and heavy impact.Forms: Practices pre-arranged patterns called kata to simulate combat against multiple opponents.Taekwondo TechniquesKicking Dominance: Dedicates 70% to 80% of its system to legs, using fast roundhouse kicks (dollyo chagi), axe kicks, and spinning hook kicks.Acrobatics: Features high-impact jumping and spinning techniques designed for speed and agility.Hand Backup: Employs punches (jirugi) primarily for close-range defense or as secondary combos.Stances: Keeps a lighter, more fluid, and bouncy stance to react quickly and maintain distance.
